summary: Defines the Host Resources MIB for managing host computers, covering things such as storage, processes and installed software. It clarifies the earlier version based on implementation experience and moves to the SMIv2 format. It is a standards-track document at the draft standard level.

eli5.summary: This lets management software ask a computer what it has inside, like disk space and running programs.

subtitle: A standard SNMP MIB for asking a computer about its memory, disks, devices, running programs and installed software.

tldr.problem: Network managers need a uniform way to manage host computers, whatever their operating system, network services or applications.
tldr.mechanism: The Host Resources MIB defines objects under mib-2 25 in groups for system, storage, devices, running software, running software performance and installed software, so one SNMP query style works on any host.
tldr.outcome: This revision clarifies the original based on implementation and deployment experience and rewrites it in SMIv2 format, while staying semantically identical. It obsoletes RFC 1514.

today: RFC 2790 is a Draft Standard published in March 2000 and obsoletes RFC 1514. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
The Host Resources MIB defines a uniform set of objects for managing host computers. The RFC uses "host" for any computer that communicates with other similar computers on the internet and is directly used by one or more human beings, such as personal computers and systems running variants of Unix. It may be relevant to devices whose main job is communications, such as routers, but that is not the focus.

The objects are independent of operating system, network services or any software application, and are common across many computer architectures. Objects in the SNMPv2-MIB and IF-MIB also help with host management, and implementing the System and Interfaces groups is mandatory for implementors of the Host Resources MIB.
sections.eli5: It works for any ordinary computer that a person uses, whether it is a PC or a Unix machine, and does not care what programs are on it.

sections.title: The Seven Groups
sections.content:
Everything sits under host, which is { mib-2 25 }. It has seven branches: hrSystem, hrStorage, hrDevice, hrSWRun, hrSWRunPerf, hrSWInstalled and hrMIBAdminInfo.

The MIB also defines three textual conventions. KBytes is a storage size in units of 1024 bytes. ProductID identifies the manufacturer, model and version of a hardware or software product, and the RFC suggests registering products so that all products from one manufacturer share a subtree. InternationalDisplayString models text in some character set.
sections.eli5: The computer's information is kept in seven labelled drawers: the system, storage, devices, running programs, how busy programs are, installed programs and some admin notes.

sections.title: System, Storage and Devices
sections.content:
The System group reports things like hrSystemUptime (time since the host was last initialized, which differs from sysUpTime), hrSystemDate, the number of user sessions, the number of processes and the maximum number of processes. Writing the initial-load objects only changes the configuration used the next time the operating system loads and does not cause a reload.

The Storage group has hrMemorySize for physical read-write main memory and the hrStorageTable of logical storage areas, such as disk partitions, file systems, RAM and swap space. Each entry has a type, description, allocation unit size, size, amount used and a count of allocation failures. The table is meant as a diagnostic for out-of-memory and out-of-buffers failures, and for tracking memory, disk or buffer usage.

The Device group has an hrDeviceTable with an index, type, description, product ID, status and error count for each device. For processors, network interfaces, printers and disk drives, extra device-specific tables hold more detail. The HOST-RESOURCES-TYPES module registers device types such as hrDeviceProcessor, hrDeviceNetwork, hrDevicePrinter and hrDeviceDiskStorage.
sections.eli5: You can ask how long the computer has been on, how much memory and disk space it has and how full they are, and what parts, like the processor or printer, it is made of.

sections.title: Running and Installed Software
sections.content:
The Running Software group lists each piece of software running on the host in hrSWRunTable: its name, product ID, path, parameters, type and status. The status is one of running (1), runnable (2, waiting for a resource such as CPU, memory or I/O), notRunnable (3, loaded but waiting for an event) or invalid (4, not loaded). The status is writable, and setting it to invalid causes the software to stop running and be unloaded. Other values may not be set.

The Running Software Performance group adds a table with one entry per running item, with the CPU resources it has consumed and the real system memory allocated to it.

The Installed Software group lists software stored locally in long-term storage such as a disk. It does not include software loaded from a network server, so not every running program appears in it. It also has objects recording when the table last changed and was last updated, which helps managers because caching the table is a popular implementation approach.
sections.eli5: You can ask which programs are running right now and which are just sitting on the disk. You can even tell a running program to stop.

sections.title: Internationalization
sections.content:
Many objects hold file-system pathnames. File systems may allow pathnames in character sets other than ASCII but often do not record which one is used. Agents are generally not configured for the right character set for every file, so the MIB could not require the agent to tag each pathname with its character set.

The solution is the InternationalDisplayString textual convention, which can carry multi-byte encodings. A management station should use a local algorithm to decide which character set is in use, relying on human configuration much as a program running on the host would. A size limit on such an object counts octets, not encoded symbols.
sections.eli5: Names of files can be written in many alphabets, and the computer does not always say which one. So the person looking picks the alphabet to read them in.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The MIB defines types for storage, devices and file systems, used as values of hrStorageType, hrDeviceType and hrFSType. New computing technologies need new types, so the IANA is the registration authority for registrations beyond those in the RFC and maintains the HOST-RESOURCES-TYPES module.

To avoid two registrations for the same technology, for instance one known by a name and an acronym, applications for new types are reviewed by a Designated Expert appointed by the IESG.
sections.eli5: When a new kind of gadget appears, a librarian adds it to the shared list, after an expert checks that it is not already there under another name.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 1514
sections.content:
This revision of 6 March 2000 clarifies and fixes the first version based on implementation experience, and it was reformatted into SMIv2 while remaining semantically identical to the SMIv1-based MIB. Changes include the new RFC boilerplate, a Security Considerations section, an IANA considerations section and an Internationalization Considerations section.

The syntax moved to SMIv2 types and macros, and new textual conventions were adopted: TruthValue, DateAndTime, AutonomousType and InterfaceIndexOrZero. The RFC also fixed a typo in hrPrinterStatus, added missing error bits to hrPrinterDetectedErrorState, and clarified the use of a dozen objects, including hrMemorySize, hrStorageSize, hrProcessorLoad and hrSWRunStatus.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition. It fixes confusing bits that people found when they actually used it, and writes it in a newer format.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some objects have read-write access, and allowing SET operations without protection can harm system operation. Other objects can be sensitive. The Running Software group reveals what software, including operating system and version, runs on the system, and an inventory of versions may help an attacker who wants to exploit bugs. The same applies to the Installed Software group.

It is therefore important to control even GET access to these objects, and possibly to encrypt their values on the wire. SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, and not all SNMP versions provide the needed features. The RFC recommends implementers consider SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). Configuring the SNMP entity so only legitimate users can GET or SET the objects is left to the user.
sections.eli5: A list of everything running on a computer is useful to a burglar too. So only people who should see it ought to be allowed to ask.
